lines: A random pivot means quicksort takes a different number of comparisons on the very same input, run after run.
What this topic computes is the exact average of that number, in one line, with nothing solved recursively.
Think about the shape of the answer before the exact number arrives: does doubling the size roughly double the cost, or square it?
answer: Two n times the natural log of n is the right shape; what comes next is the exact correction sitting on top of it.

lines: The expectation of a sum always equals the sum of the expectations, and that holds whether or not the pieces are related.
Two draws from an urn without replacement are related, since the first draw changes what is left for the second, and the rule still holds.
Give one event a variable that is one when it happens and zero otherwise, and that variable's average is just the event's probability.
Any count built out of such variables turns, by linearity, into nothing more than a sum of probabilities.
Shuffle anything and ask how many items land back in their own starting spot: on average, exactly one does, no matter how large the set is.
Whether one position staying fixed makes another position more or less likely to stay fixed does not matter at all to this sum.
Line the keys up by rank, and ask when two of them, however far apart in rank, ever get compared to each other.
They get compared exactly when the very first pivot chosen from everything ranked between them turns out to be one of the two themselves.
Add that probability up over every possible pair of ranks, and the sum is the exact expected number of comparisons, not an estimate of it.
It sits close to the earlier guess of two n times the natural log of n, but with a correction that is exact rather than approximate.
An earlier topic reached this identical number by writing down a recurrence over how the algorithm recurses on smaller pieces.
Reaching the same number from a probability per pair, with no recursion at all, is confirmation that both routes describe one real quantity.
Draw coupons with replacement and keep going until every distinct one has turned up at least once.
Split that wait into one phase per newly seen coupon; each phase waits geometrically, and linearity adds all those waits into a single harmonic sum.
That average describes the whole population of runs, not the particular run you happen to be watching.
It says nothing by itself about how far a single run can land from the average, or how rarely that happens.
Fixed points, quicksort's comparisons, and the coupon collector's draws are three unrelated-looking counts.
Every one of them turned into a sum of probabilities the moment it was written as a sum of indicator variables, dependence or none.
